title: Why Our Neighborhoods Bake (and How to Cool Them Down)

speaker.persona: City planner of twelve years who runs neighborhood workshops; friendly, digressive, full of bike-ride and family stories

outlineText:
Welcome and why this matters to me
What makes cities hotter
  Pavement and dark roofs [cues: asphalt, blacktop]
  Too few trees
  Heat trapped after sunset
Health effects
  Heat stroke and dehydration
  Sleepless nights and heart strain
Cooling strategies
  Street trees and shade
  Cool roofs and pale surfaces
  Water features [cues: splash pads, fountains]
Equity: who gets hit hardest
Community action

segments.say: Hey everyone, thanks for squeezing in. It's a little stuffy in here, which is kind of perfect for tonight. I'm Rosa, I've been a planner with the city for twelve years.
And honestly, why I got obsessed with this is personal. My grandmother lived on the fourth floor of a walk-up with no air conditioning, and every August we'd take shifts sitting with her.
Side note, she also made the best iced tea on the planet, dangerously sweet, and she took the recipe to her grave, which I'm still a little bitter about.
Anyway, she's gonna come up again later when we talk about which neighborhoods end up carrying the load.
Okay. So. Let's, uh, let's dig in.
So first off, why is downtown such an oven? Bike in from the farms on a summer afternoon and you feel it, the core runs seven to ten degrees warmer, and it's all stuff we built.

Start with the ground under your feet. Picture a big box store parking lot in July, that black tar drinks in sunlight all day, I once watched a guy fry an egg on one. Same with the tar-paper tops of the buildings downtown.
Um, hang on, I had a number for this somewhere, sorry, my notes are, uh, a mess. Okay, never mind.
The other half is what's missing. Walk down any older block on the east side and look up, there's barely any canopy, just bare sky and a couple of scraggly saplings in concrete boxes.
Leaves are nature's air conditioner, they block the sun and sweat moisture into the air, and when those neighborhoods got paved over, the big old oaks and elms came down and never came back.
And that ties back to the parking lot thing I mentioned, same block, bare ground on the bottom, no branches overhead.

Now here's the part people don't expect. Once the sun goes down, all that brick and concrete keeps giving off the warmth it stored, like a pizza stone out of the oven, so downtown is still eighty-something at dawn.
Alright, um, so, moving along.
So why should you care, besides being sweaty and grumpy? It's the deadliest weather we get, it quietly kills more people than hurricanes or floods, and it goes after your body two different ways.

The fast, scary version is when your body can't shed the warmth anymore, usually after sweating all day without drinking enough, you get confused and dizzy, your temperature spikes, sometimes you stop sweating, and that's an emergency, you call nine one one.
Totally random, but my first ribbon cutting photo is still on our website, I've got bangs, please don't look it up.
The slower damage is sneakier. When your bedroom never drops below eighty, you toss and turn, you never really rest, and your pulse and blood pressure stay up, so the E R sees more chest pains.
And that's why the stored-up warmth from the bricks I talked about is such a big deal, it won't let your body reset.
Sorry, is the mic okay? Can the back hear me? Okay, thumbs up, great. Um, where was I.
So what do we actually do about it? The good news is we already know the fixes, and a lot of them are pretty cheap, it's mostly about follow-through.
Number one, and you knew I'd say this, plant. Oaks, maples, honey locusts along the sidewalks, with enough room for the roots so they survive past year three.
A big leafy canopy over a block can knock the temperature underneath way down, and people will literally cross the road to walk under it, we did counts.
My neighbor is at war with the squirrels, he bought a fake owl, and now the squirrels just sit on the owl, so, nature wins again.
Okay, and then the fun one, kids love this. Spray grounds, misting stations, hydrants with those sprinkler caps, even a drinking tap in the park helps people ride out a bad afternoon.
And there's a whole question of which parks get this stuff, which I'll get to in a few minutes, because spoiler, it's not spread out evenly.
We daylighted a creek by the rail yard, pulled it out of an old pipe, and on a scorching day that corridor feels a good five degrees nicer.
Okay, um, so, next thing.
Put a satellite map of afternoon temperatures next to a map of income and they line up almost perfectly. The poorer blocks, a lot of them redlined back in the thirties, are the ones baking.
Which is basically my grandmother's building, like I said at the start, fourth floor, no air conditioning, nothing green out front.
Oh shoot, wait, I skipped right over one of the fixes, the one on top of the buildings. Okay, back up a sec.
You can paint the top of a building white, or put on a reflective membrane, and instead of soaking up the sun it bounces most of that light back to the sky.
On a July afternoon a black one can reach a hundred and fifty degrees and a white one runs something like fifty less, and whoever lives on the top floor feels it.
Okay, so, back to who's stuck with the worst of it, because that's where those rooftop programs should be going first.
Fair warning, before you leave I'm putting every one of you to work on this, but we're not quite there yet.
Renters can't repaint the building or plant in a yard they don't own, and people working outside can't just stay in all day, so the burden lands on the folks with the least say.
So here's my ask. Organize your block. Sign up for the free sapling giveaway in the spring, and then actually water the thing, like twenty gallons a week for two summers.
Check on your neighbors when it's brutal out, especially anyone living alone, and show up to budget hearings and ask for your block to go first, because the squeaky wheel does get funded.
